يونيسف: 67% من أسر السودان تعاني انعدام الأمن المائي - عاجل
sudan.content: يونيسف: 67% من الأسر في السودان تعاني انعدام الأمن المائي تخطّي إلى المحتوى صحيفة عاجل الإلكترونية النشرة البريدية اتصل بنا تابعنا: ابحث في عاجل… اللغات الرئيسية المحليات الاقتصاد رياضة مدارات عالمية وظائف الترفيه منوعات سياحة وسفر مجتمع كل الأقسام الرئيسية ‹ مدارات عالمية ‹ الخبر مدارات عالمية دقيقة قراءة يونيسف: 67% من أسر السودان تعاني انعدام الأمن المائي فريق التحرير نُشر في الأربعاء 21 أكتوبر 2026 · 2:23 م ملخّص إيجاز بالذكاء الاصطناعي أخبار ذات علاقة مركز الملك سلمان للإغاثة يوزّع 6,513 سلة غذائية على أسر نازحة في 12 مخيمًا باليمن الإثنين 19 أكتوبر 2026 مجلس الأمن يدعو إلى حماية الأطفال من مخاطر التكنولوجيا الرقمية الثلاثاء 20 أكتوبر 2026 حقوقي يمني: اعتداءات الميليشيا الحوثية على المدنيين بالمملكة انتهاك يستوجب المساءلة الدولية الإثنين 19 أكتوبر 2026 صحفي يمني: تصاعد الاصطفاف ضد الحوثيين.. والميليشيا تمارس التجويع الإثنين 19 أكتوبر 2026 النشرة البريدية أهم الأخبار إلى بريدك كل صباح. بريدك الإلكتروني اشترك الآن اسأل الخبر مساعد ذكي يجيب من سياق الخبر فقط اسأل ما تريد عن هذا الخبر ما الفكرة الرئيسية للخبر؟ ما هي أبرز الأرقام والإحصاءات؟ كيف يؤثر هذا علي؟ صحيفة إلكترونية سعودية تم تأسيسها عام 2007م تهتم بنشر الأخبار المحلية والمنافسة في سبق الأخبار بمهنية ومصداقية وموضوعية ★ اجعل «عاجل» مصدرك المفضل في قوقل الأقسام المحليات الاقتصاد رياضة مدارات عالمية وظائف الترفيه روابط سريعة الرئيسية مقالات الرأي البحث النشرة البريدية الصحيفة من نحن اتصل بنا أعلن معنا سياسة الخصوصية جميع الحقوق محفوظة لـ شركة إيجاز للنشر الإلكتروني المالكة لصحيفة عاجل شروط الاستخدام أعلنت منظمة الأمم المتحدة للطفولة (يونيسف) ومجموعة المياه والصرف الصحي والنظافة التابعة للأمم المتحدة أن 67% من الأسر في السودان تعاني انعدام الأمن المائي. وذكرت المنظمتان في تقرير استند إلى نتائج التقييم متعدد القطاعات للاحتياجات، الذي أُجري في يوليو 2026، أن 41.2% من الأسر تفتقر إلى خدمات المياه الأساسية، بينما تفتقر 53.7% إلى الحد الأدنى من خدمات الصرف الصحي، و46.8% إلى خدمات النظافة الأساسية. اقرأ أيضًا: مركز الملك سلمان للإغاثة يضخ 60 ألف لتر من مياه الشرب في مديرية المظفر بتعز وأوضح التقرير أن المسح شمل 23,736 أسرة في جميع ولايات السودان، ورصد مستويات الخدمات المتوفرة ومظاهر انعدام الأمن المائي وأساليب التكيف التي تعتمدها الأسر لمواجهة نقص المياه، إضافة إلى العوائق التي تحول دون تلبية احتياجاتها من المياه والصرف الصحي. ناقش الخبر مع الذكاء الاصطناعي ChatGPT Gemini Claude Grok وَرَد في الخبر مكان السودان تابع القراءة اقرأ أيضًا مدارات عالمية الأحد 18 أكتوبر 2026 تقرير حقوقي يوثق ارتكاب الحوثيين 170 انتهاكًا في 9 محافظات يمنية خلال 48 ساعة اقرأ التالي مدارات عالمية الإثنين 19 أكتوبر 2026 مدير مطار الخرطوم: الهجمات بالمسيرات لم تؤثر في حركة الطيران اقرأ التالي مدارات عالمية الإثنين 19 أكتوبر 2026 «مسام» ينزع 995 من الألغام والذخائر غير المنفجرة والعبوات الناسفة في اليمن خلال أسبوع اقرأ التالي الاقتصاد الأربعاء 21 أكتوبر 2026 أمانة القصيم تسلّم 200 وحدة سكنية ضمن الإسكان التنموي خلال الربع الثالث اقرأ التالي مدارات عالمية الأربعاء 21 أكتوبر 2026 مركز الملك سلمان للإغاثة يضخ المياه الصالحة للشرب في محافظتي تعز ولحج اقرأ التالي مدارات عالمية الإثنين 19 أكتوبر رفضاً لإخلاء داخلية أبو دجانة أمستردام: الخرطوم: كمبالا / الأربعاء 21 أكتوبر 2026 توافد طلاب من كلية الهندسة وكليات أخرى بجامعة الخرطوم إلى داخلية أبو دجانة، تضامناً مع زملائهم المقيمين فيها، واحتجاجاً على قرار إدارة الجامعة والصندوق القومي لرعاية الطلاب بإخلاء المبنى ونقلهم إلى مجمع كلية التربية بأم درمان، لإفساح المجال أمام إسكان الطالبات بصورة مؤقتة. و ظلت داخلية أبو دجانة تاريخياً مخصصة بصورة أساسية لطلاب الهندسة في المستويات الثالث والرابع والخامس، واقتصر السكن فيها خلال بعض السنوات على طلاب المستويين الرابع والخامس. ومع اقتراب موعد استئناف الدراسة بالكلية في 24 أكتوبر الجاري، يواجه طلاب الداخلية، أعباء إضافية تتمثل في الانتقال إلى مجمع كلية التربية بأم درمان، والتنقل يومياً إلى كليتهم بالخرطوم، بتكلفة مواصلات قد تصل إلى نحو 14 ألف جنيه سوداني للطالب يومياً، وفقاً لمنصة جامعة الخرطوم، في ظل عدم توفير الإدارة، وسيلة ترحيل منتظمة بين المجمعين. وأوضح مصدر مطلع بالجامعة أن الداخلية شهدت خلال الفترة الماضية أعمال صيانة وتأهيل بمبادرات من الجمعية الهندسية التسييرية، وبمساهمات من مهندسين وخريجين، ورجح أن تكون جاهزية أبو دجانة أحد الأسباب التي دفعت الجهات المعنية إلى اختيارها لإسكان الطالبات مؤقتاً. رفض للقرار وبحسب بيان صادر عن لجنة طلاب داخلية أبو دجانة، اطلعت عليه (دبنقا)، رفض الطلاب القرار وتمسكوا بالبقاء في غرفهم، مشككين في إمكانية العودة خلال الفترة المحددة التي تتراوح بين 15 و20 يوماً، مستندين إلى تجارب سابقة لإخلاء داخليات البركس والوسط، إلى جانب داخلية عبد السلام بشمبات، التي قالوا إن طلابها أُخرجوا منها دون توفير بديل. من جانبها أعلنت الجمعية الهندسية التسييرية بكلية الهندسة رفضها الكامل لقرار الإخلاء، ودعت طلاب الكلية إلى البقاء في الداخلية وعدم الاستجابة لطلبات المغادرة، معتبرة أن الخطوة تعكس عدم اكتمال استعدادات الجامعة لاستقبال الطلاب والطالبات. ودعت اللجنة الطلاب إلى مواصلة التواجد في الداخلية، محذرة من احتمال محاولة تنفيذ قرار الإخلاء بالقوة، في وقت لا تزال فيه الأزمة دون حسم، وسط مطالبات لإدارة الجامعة والصندوق القومي لرعاية الطلاب بإيجاد حلول تضمن حقوق جميع الطلاب والطالبات. أنه لا مكان لمن وصفهم بالعملاء وادي حلفا، 21 أكتوبر 2026 – قال رئيس مجلس السيادة الانتقالي، القائد العام للجيش السوداني، عبد الفتاح البرهان، الثلاثاء، إنه لن يكون هناك مكان في السودان لمن وصفهم بالعملاء، مؤكداً رفضه لأي محاولة لفرض حكم على السودانيين من الخارج. وأفاد البرهان لدى مخاطبته حشداً جماهيرياً بمدينة وادي حلفا في الولاية الشمالية بأن «السودان مفتوح أمام جميع أبنائه، إذا أردت الاحترام تعال إلى الداخل»، وأعلن رفضه محاولات الوصول إلى السلطة عبر العمالة أو الاستقواء بالخارج. وتابع: «مافي زول بقدر يتسلط على الشعب السوداني، لا حمدوك بجي ولا قحت بتجي، زول بشيل سلاح من برة يجي يحكمنا إلا نكون مافي»، في إشارة إلى رفضه عودة القوى السياسية إلى الحكم بدعم خارجي أو فرض إرادتها على السودانيين. وجدد البرهان موقفه الرافض للتفاوض مع قوات الدعم السريع، قائلاً إن التمرد لا مجال للحوار معه، وإن الخيار أمامه هو إلقاء السلاح والاستسلام، أو مواصلة العمليات العسكرية ضده. كما وجه رسالة إلى الجهات التي قال إنها تحرض على السودان، داعياً إياها إلى الحضور إلى الداخل، ومؤكداً أن أي طرف لن يستطيع فرض إرادته على البلاد من الخارج. وشدد رئيس مجلس السيادة على أنه لا وصاية على الشعب السوداني أو الجيش، وأن اختيار من يحكم البلاد يجب أن يتم عبر الانتخابات، قائلاً إن «الرأي في النهاية للشعب السوداني». وطمأن البرهان المواطنين بشأن مستقبل البلاد، وأكد أن الدولة ستواصل مسيرتها وأن السودان سيمضي إلى الأمام، داعياً السودانيين إلى عدم الخوف أو القلق على مستقبل الدولة. وفي سياق متصل، أعرب البرهان عن شكره لجمهورية مصر العربية، مؤكداً أن المواطنين المصريين في السودان «في أمان وما عندهم مشكلة»، ومشدداً على أهمية استمرار التواصل بين البلدين وتقوية المصالح المشتركة. الكلمات: عبد الفتاح البرهان، وادي حلفا، مجلس السيادة، الجيش السوداني، الدعم السريع، رفض التفاوض، الانتخابات، حمدوك، قحت، الحرب في السودان مقالات ذات صلة «الحرية والتغيير» ترحب بالتحقيق الدولي وتدعو لاستكماله بالإحالة لـ بمحلية الطينة بولاية شمال دارفور إن «متطوعَين في العمل الإنساني وثلاثة نازحين قُتلوا جراء قصف جوي استهدف مساء الثلاثاء منطقة بامنا، فيما أصيب عدد من المدنيين بإصابات خطرة». وتقع بلدة «بامنا» داخل الأراضي التشادية، حيث لجأ إليها آلاف المواطنين السودانيين من مناطق الطينة وأمبرو وكرنوي بولاية شمال دارفور جراء الهجمات التي تشنها قوات الدعم السريع. وأفاد البيان أن القصف أسفر عن مقتل الهادي صندل عيسى، منسق غرفة طوارئ بامنا، والمتطوع آدم عمدة عرجة، عضو مكتب البرامج، إلى جانب ثلاثة من النازحين المقيمين بمراكز الإيواء في المنطقة. وأشار إلى أن عدداً من المدنيين أصيبوا بجروح خطرة جراء القصف، لافتاً إلى أن الانقطاع التام للاتصالات يزيد من صعوبة متابعة الأوضاع الميدانية والاطمئنان على المصابين. وحذّر المجلس من تداعيات استهداف المناطق المأهولة بالمدنيين ومراكز إيواء النازحين، مؤكداً أن مثل هذه الهجمات تفاقم معاناة السكان الذين أنهكتهم الحرب والنزوح، ومشدداً على ضرورة حماية المدنيين والعاملين في المجال الإنساني وضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية بصورة آمنة. ولم يحمّل المجلس أي جهة مسؤولية الوقوف وراء الحادثة، ولكن متطوعين في منطقة الطينة اتهموا قوات الدعم السريع بقصف اللاجئين السودانيين، ضمن موجة تصعيد جوي استهدف أماكن تجمعاتهم في المناطق الحدودية بين السودان وتشاد. وسبق أن اتُّهمت قوات الدعم السريع بتجاوز الحدود السودانية والتوغل داخل الأراضي التشادية في أكثر من ثلاث مناسبات شملت توغلات برية وهجمات على معسكرات للجيش التشادي، إلى جانب هجمات بطائرات مسيّرة استهدفت مدنيين سودانيين داخل الأراضي التشادية. وأقرت قوات الدعم السريع بمسؤوليتها عن بعض تلك الهجمات، قبل أن تعتذر عنها وتقول إنها وقعت عن طريق الخطأ أثناء مطاردة مسلحين سودانيين. ومنذ أشهر، تدور معارك عنيفة بين الجيش السوداني وحلفائه في القوة المشتركة من جهة، وقوات الدعم السريع من جهة أخرى، في مناطق الطينة وأمبرو وكرنوي بولاية شمال دارفور، في ظل مساعي الدعم السريع للسيطرة على المواقع المتبقية للجيش في إقليم دارفور، فيما يواصل الجيش والقوات المتحالفة معه الدفاع عن مواقعهم في المنطقة الحدودية مع تشاد. الكلمات: لاجئون سودانيون، تشاد، الطينة، شمال دارفور، بامنا، قصف بمسيّرة، عمال الإغاثة، غرف الطوارئ، الدعم ethiopia.content: Africa: Ethiopia Calls for Data-Driven Policymaking to Accelerate Africa's Progress - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Ethiopia Calls for Data-Driven Policymaking to Accelerate Africa's Progress 21 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia has reformed its statistical legislation and established an independent statistical service to strengthen the production and coordination of official data, President Taye Atske Selassie said. Taye underscored the importance of reliable statistics in driving evidence-based development in Africa. Addressing the opening of the 10th Session of the Statistical Commission for Africa and the 12th Meeting of the Regional Committee of the United Nations Global Geospatial Information Management for Africa in Addis Ababa, the President said Ethiopia's development planning is anchored in measurable targets and reliable data. He emphasized that development cannot be effectively planned, sustained, or scaled up without accurate measurement, noting that official statistics are essential for shaping development strategies, tracking progress, and strengthening accountability. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The President also highlighted Ethiopia's reforms in the financial and digital sectors, including the National Digital Payment Strategy, financial sector liberalization, interoperable payment infrastructure, and the national digital identification program, Fayda. He said Fayda enables secure electronic verification and expands access to banking, mobile money, telecommunications, and other essential public services, demonstrating how digital infrastructure can improve service delivery and financial inclusion. According to the President, mobile money and mobile banking accounts in Ethiopia reached 257 million and processed more than 24 trillion birr in transactions during the first nine months of 2026, reflecting the expansion of the country's financial and digital systems. Drawing lessons from these reforms, he stressed that statistics must serve as practical tools for sustainable development and be communicated clearly and accessibly to policymakers and citizens, rather than being treated as an end in themselves. He also called for statistical institutions to integrate and safeguard diverse data sources without compromising statistical integrity, emphasizing that innovation must reinforce data quality, institutional independence, and public trust. The President urged African governments to protect the professional independence of official statistics, strengthen legal and institutional frameworks, invest in national statistical systems, and ground policy decisions in scientific evidence. He cautioned that poor-quality data undermines evidence-based policymaking, impedes development, and weakens accountability. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: News - Funding Shortfalls Threaten Health Services in Ethiopia's Conflict-Hit Regions, UN Warns - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: News - Funding Shortfalls Threaten Health Services in Ethiopia's Conflict-Hit Regions, UN Warns 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Funding shortages threaten essential health and nutrition services in Ethiopia's conflict-affected regions, with 10 of the 16 operational mobile health and nutrition teams in Amhara expected to shut down by the end of October, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said. According to OCHA , only 16 of the 57 mobile health and nutrition teams required in Amhara are currently operational. Of these, 10 are expected to cease operations by the end of the month because of funding constraints. Humanitarian partners are continuing to deliver life-saving assistance despite insecurity and access challenges in parts of northern Ethiopia, including Tigray, Amhara and Afar, the UN agency said. In Tigray, additional medical, nutrition and other essential supplies have reached communities and health facilities, with further deliveries expected. Humanitarian partners are also working with regional authorities to facilitate access and expand assistance. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn On Tuesday, Humanitarian Coordinator in Ethiopia Ozonnia Ojielo met officials from the newly established caretaker interim administration in Tigray, emphasizing the need for unhindered humanitarian access, according to OCHA. In Amhara, humanitarian partners are preparing to provide food assistance to approximately 100,000 people in Wag Hamra and North Wollo zones. Operations are also continuing in Afar, although limited funding remains a major obstacle to expanding the response. OCHA said humanitarian needs across Ethiopia continue to exceed available resources, warning that funding shortfalls are undermining efforts to sustain essential services for vulnerable communities. The agency reiterated its call for all parties to facilitate the expansion of life-saving humanitarian assistance and ensure humanitarian actors can reach people in need. The funding shortfall extends beyond health services, affecting food assistance, refugee protection and support for internally displaced people (IDPs), as previously reported by Addis Standard. Earlier this month, Addis Standard reported that IDPs in camps in Debre Birhan were facing worsening shortages of food, medicines, healthcare and other essential services as humanitarian organizations scaled back or withdrew operations amid funding constraints. Continued displacement from conflict-affected areas has further strained already limited resources. The situation reflects a broader displacement crisis across Amhara. As of early 2025, more than 660,000 people were estimated to be living in 31 IDP sites and collective centres across seven administrative zones, with North and South Wollo accounting for approximately 55% of the sites. Major displacement locations include the Bakelo and China camps in Debre Birhan and the Jara IDP Centre in North Wollo. ethiopia.title: Eritrea Tells Us There Is No 'Crisis' Between Ethiopia and Eritrea
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Eritrea Tells Us There Is No 'Crisis' Between Ethiopia and Eritrea - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Eritrea Tells Us There Is No 'Crisis' Between Ethiopia and Eritrea 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Eritrea's Ambassador to the United Nations, Sophia Tesfamariam, has told senior US diplomats that there is no "crisis" between Ethiopia and Eritrea, while urging Washington and other international actors to address what she described as threats to Eritrea's sovereignty and territorial integrity. In a statement posted on X on 20 October, Sophia said she held "constructive engagements" with Mike Waltz, the US permanent representative to the UN, and Jeffrey Bartos, the US representative to the UN for Management and Reform, to discuss developments in the Horn of Africa and present Asmara's position on the region's deteriorating security situation. Over the last two weeks, the two countries exchanged accusations at the United Nations over their deteriorating relations. Ethiopia sent a letter to the UN Security Council in early October accusing Eritrean forces of an "all-out invasion" of parts of Tigray in northern Ethiopia and invoking its right to self-defence. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Eritrea rejected Ethiopia's account and, in its own communication to the Council, accused Addis Abeba of threatening a war of aggression over Red Sea access. The two governments' competing accounts have emerged alongside renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia and heightened fears of a broader regional conflict. Sophia said she had "reiterated that there is no 'crisis' between Eritrea and Ethiopia" and argued that the international community should pay closer attention to developments within Ethiopia. She urged Addis Abeba to "respect Eritrea's sovereign territories and stop diverting attention from its domestic issues." The ambassador also accused Ethiopia of pursuing a three-year campaign concerning access to the Red Sea and making continued threats against Eritrea's sovereignty, including what she described as threats to annex Eritrean territory. She called on countries with influence in the region to act "responsibly and proactively" to prevent a wider conflict, cautioning them against making statements that could embolden Ethiopia's leadership. "Eritrea's sovereignty and territorial integrity must be respected," she said, adding that preventing renewed conflict requires addressing underlying threats, upholding international law and acting before tensions escalate. Credit: Office of the Prime Minister of Ethiopia Diplomatic tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea remain unresolved despite international appeals for restraint, with the neighboring countries continuing to exchange accusations over territorial security, armed opposition groups and access to the Red Sea. The confrontation has intensified following Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s October 19 warning that Eritrea could face severe consequences if it continued providing support to groups opposing his government. In a Tigrigna-language interview broadcast by Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), Abiy accused Eritrea of allowing its territory to serve as a base for forces hostile to Ethiopia while maintaining that peaceful cooperation remained possible. The remarks, detailed in Kulu Media’s report on Abiy’s warning , came amid renewed military operations in Tigray and heightened concern over the possibility of a wider regional confrontation. Eritrea has rejected Ethiopian accusations of supporting armed opposition groups. Asmara has instead accused Addis Ababa of threatening its sovereignty through demands for greater access to the Red Sea. International Pressure for De-escalation The United States and United Kingdom have urged both governments to avoid further escalation and resolve their differences through diplomacy. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for restraint during discussions with Abiy Ahmed, emphasizing respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity. The United Kingdom subsequently urged renewed diplomatic engagement and expressed support for African Union efforts to reduce tensions. As detailed in Kulu Media’s coverage of the UK’s diplomatic appeal , London also warned about the humanitarian consequences of renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia. The Associated Press reported that international concerns have increased as renewed fighting in Tigray places additional pressure on the fragile security arrangements established after the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. Competing Claims Over Border Security Ethiopia has accused Eritrean forces of entering its territory and supporting insurgent groups, allegations Eritrea disputes. Earlier this month, Ethiopia informed the United Nations Security Council that it was invoking its right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter. Eritrea rejected that justification and accused Ethiopia of threatening its territorial integrity. The Associated Press reported that the competing allegations could not be independently verified in full. The confrontation has also been complicated by Ethiopia’s longstanding interest in securing reliable maritime access, including through arrangements involving Red Sea ports. Eritrea regards any attempt to obtain sovereign control over its territory as a threat to national sovereignty. Despite repeated international calls for dialogue, there has been no independently confirmed agreement on a new ceasefire, military withdrawal or formal bilateral negotiation process. The absence of such an agreement leaves the relationship vulnerable to further deterioration as military and political developments continue in northern Ethiopia. Published 8 minutes ago on October 21, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk File Photo: Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with US special envoy Steve Witkoff during a meeting in St. Petersburg, Russia. Credit: Sputnik / Pool / AFP-Jiji Russian President Vladimir Putin met US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Saint Petersburg on Wednesday, October 21, as Washington intensified diplomatic efforts to negotiate a ceasefire and end the war in Ukraine. During the meeting, Witkoff said there was a basis for reaching a ceasefire and urged Putin to consider restarting trilateral negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States, according to Russian news agencies Interfax and TASS, whose accounts were reported by Reuters . The American envoy proposed discussions involving technical experts from the three countries to address outstanding issues in a potential settlement. He also presented documents outlining Washington’s approach to ending the conflict. The discussions followed Witkoff’s meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European representatives in Oslo on Tuesday, where participants examined proposals covering security guarantees, energy infrastructure and possible arrangements for a ceasefire. According to Associated Press , the latest diplomatic initiative seeks to revive negotiations that have struggled to produce a breakthrough despite repeated international efforts. Russia Signals Interest in Renewed US Relations Putin thanked US President Donald Trump for his efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict and expressed Russia’s interest in restoring economic relations with Washington, according to the Russian news agencies. The Kremlin also indicated its willingness to discuss wider international issues, including tensions involving Iran. The meeting took place amid concerns among Ukrainian officials and European allies about the direction of US policy toward Russia and the terms of a potential peace agreement. Although Witkoff expressed optimism about the possibility of renewed negotiations, Russia has not publicly accepted a new ceasefire framework or confirmed a date for trilateral talks. Prisoner Release Accompanies Diplomatic Talks The diplomatic meeting coincided with Russia’s release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard, who had been imprisoned after being accused of fighting alongside Ukrainian forces. Hubbard, a former teacher from Michigan, had been detained since 2022 and was sentenced in 2024 to nearly seven years in prison. The United States previously designated him as wrongfully detained. The diplomatic initiative also follows uncertainty over American military assistance, including a temporary interruption in intelligence sharing with Ukraine that was resolved earlier this month. According to Associated Press , President Trump had personally requested Hubbard’s release. The White House said the arrangement did not require the United States to release another prisoner in exchange. The release represented a concrete diplomatic gesture during the renewed engagement between Washington and Moscow, although it did not establish progress toward a broader settlement of the war. Fighting Continues Despite Diplomatic Efforts The latest negotiations come as Russian and Ukrainian forces continue military operations, including drone and missile attacks affecting civilian areas and energy infrastructure. Ukrainian authorities reported additional casualties and damage from overnight Russian strikes on October 21, underscoring the continuing humanitarian consequences of the conflict. Ukraine has repeatedly emphasized that any lasting settlement must include credible security guarantees and protect its sovereignty. Russia and Ukraine remain divided over territorial control and the conditions necessary for ending hostilities, making a comprehensive agreement difficult despite renewed American mediation. The latest meeting has reopened discussions about a possible ceasefire, but significant questions remain over whether Moscow and Kyiv can agree on its terms. For now, the proposed resumption of trilateral negotiations represents a diplomatic opportunity rather than a confirmed breakthrough in efforts to end the war. Published 1 day ago on October 20, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed speaks during an EBC interview on October 19, 2026, in which he warned Eritrea over alleged support for armed opposition groups. Image Credit: EBC / Screenshot by Kulu Media Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has warned Eritrea of severe consequences if it continues to support armed groups opposing his government, delivering one of his clearest public warnings to the neighboring country amid renewed fighting in Tigray and growing fears of a wider regional conflict. Speaking in a Tigrigna-language interview broadcast by the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC) on Monday, October 19, Abiy accused Eritrea of allowing its territory to be used by groups hostile to Ethiopia. The prime minister said cooperation between the two countries would offer greater benefits than confrontation and warned against ignoring Ethiopia’s appeals. According to Interview , Abiy said Eritrea’s continued role as a base for Ethiopia’s adversaries would bring severe consequences. The warning marks a further escalation in rhetoric between Addis Ababa and Asmara, which severed diplomatic relations earlier this month following competing allegations of military aggression and interference in each other’s internal affairs. Ethiopia has repeatedly accused Eritrea of supporting the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and other armed opposition groups. Eritrea has rejected accusations that it is backing Ethiopian rebels and has accused Addis Ababa of pursuing hostile policies toward its sovereignty. Warning Comes Amid Renewed Tigray Conflict Abiy’s remarks followed weeks of military operations in Tigray, where Ethiopian federal forces and allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) fighters have regained control of several major towns previously held by TPLF-aligned forces. The military developments have brought Ethiopian government forces closer to Eritrea’s border, intensifying concerns that the confrontation could expand beyond Tigray. As documented in Kulu Media’s coverage of the border tensions , troop movements, disputed territorial claims and the collapse of diplomatic relations have increased the risk of direct confrontation between the two countries. Earlier in October, Ethiopia accused Eritrean troops of crossing into its territory and occupying parts of northern Tigray. The Ethiopian government subsequently invoked Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, asserting its right to self-defense. Eritrea, meanwhile, called for UN action against Ethiopia, accusing Addis Ababa of preparing military aggression. The competing accusations have not been independently established in full. Abiy Says TPLF Is Nearing Its End During the interview, Abiy also addressed the TPLF’s declining control over major towns in Tigray following the latest federal military offensive. He suggested that the organization was approaching the end of its political dominance and pledged development across the region. His comments came days after the federal government established a caretaker administration with a six-month mandate to restore public services, improve security and prepare for regional elections. The TPLF-aligned leadership has rejected the new administration, challenging its legitimacy and the authority of its decisions. Abiy urged Tigray residents to preserve unity and public institutions while preparations for a future elected administration continue. Despite the federal government’s territorial gains, the security situation remains uncertain in some parts of Tigray, and political disagreements over the region’s future remain unresolved. Ethiopia and Eritrea Remain on Opposing Diplomatic Paths Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated sharply since the two countries restored diplomatic ties in 2018. The former allies fought together against the TPLF during the 2020–2022 Tigray war, but their relationship subsequently worsened over regional security, the Pretoria peace agreement and Ethiopia’s ambitions for greater access to the Red Sea. Abiy’s latest remarks combined a warning against alleged Eritrean interference with an appeal for peaceful cooperation. He said good neighborly relations and partnership remained the appropriate path forward. International concern has also increased. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently warned of wider war and urged restraint as military tensions continued along the border. Abiy’s October 19 warning does not amount to a formal declaration of war or an announcement of a new military offensive against Eritrea. However, the direct warning from Ethiopia’s prime minister adds another layer of political tension to an already volatile confrontation, with renewed fighting in Tigray threatening to destabilize the wider Horn of Africa. ethiopia.content: The El-Alamein Quadrilateral and the Risks of Geopolitical Polarization in the North East Africa – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-21 The El-Alamein Quadrilateral and the Risks of Geopolitical Polarization in the North East Africa 0 Comments The rapid changes that are taking place in the North East Africa region shake the very foundation of the post-1991 geopolitical arrangement imposed on the Horn of Africa, Nile Basin and Red Sea. Ethiopia’s civilizational, cultural and national resilience is reshaping the regional geo-economic map linking the Nile Basin, Horn of Africa and Red Sea into one strategic theater. The operationalization of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam Nile (GERD) rewrites the geopolitical mathematics of the Nile with reason and fairness. Ethiopia’s emergence as a geo-economic game-changer in the geo-economically dormant terrain of the region activates the countries to utilize the waters of the Nile for their prosperity. South Sudan seeing this trend is intending to construct the Fula Dam to power its economy and safeguard its water security. Ethiopia, questioning the legitimacy of past decisions that deprived her of access to the sea, facing chokepoint wars, and anticipating maritime blockades, goes on striving for a durable access to the sea through a reasonable and fair manner. The new breed of leadership seeks to peacefully and legally redress the 1991 injustice that makes Ethiopia landlocked. This illegitimate act was undertaken by the late Egyptian Secretary-General of the UN Boutros Boutros-Ghali in league with the TPLF-Ethiopia and PFDJ-Eritrea. The strategic sea changes in the region re-graphing the “geo” of the Nile and Red Sea disputes Egypt’s regional vision built on absolute security architecture. The fundamental change in the basic structures of the regional system has forced Egyptian officials to stop the geopolitical rebalancing of the Horn. Egypt’s Foreign Minister authoring a commentary on News24 in 2025 underlined that Egypt is using its defense and diplomatic machinery to restore its dominium on the “two of the most important axes of Egyptian national security”—Nile Basin and Red Sea. Egypt’s militaristic and diplomatic posture took shape in October 2026 in El-Alamein, forming a Quadrilateral Security Grouping that includes PFDJ-Eritrea, SAF-Sudan and Hassan Sheikh-Somalia. The grouping seeks to re-configure the complicated waters of the Nile and Red Sea without Ethiopia. Egypt which is the brain behind this unilateral governance enterprise chariots the grouping to run the sovereignty of PFDJ-Eritrea, SAF-Sudan and Hassan Sheik-Somalia through Cairo. For Ethiopia, the significance of this assemblage lies not simply in the number of participating states, but in the implications of their emerging military and intelligence coordination for the region’s wider security architecture. The grouping defines Ethiopia as a structural challenger to the alliance and Egypt’s primacy in the region. The emerging security alliance advances Egypt’s Ethiopia strategy which is designed to exploit internal political differences through exporting instabilities. PFJD-Eritrea serves as a liaison in this project. The grouping seeks to promote the dismemberment scenario gaining meaning in the form of Tsimido materially steered by Egypt and PFDJ-Eritrea. This scenario seeking to embroil Ethiopia in “forever wars” intends to control the headwaters of Abay (Blue Nile) and decouple Addis Ababa from the Red Sea. This scenario is being countered by Ethiopia. Ethiopia’s military success, confusing the El-Alamein grouping and surprising the international commentariat, shows Ethiopia cannot be treated as a challenge to be contained but as a concrete pillar of the regional order built on indivisible security paired with open economic architecture. Besides the continued military and intelligence support, the El-Alamein grouping now turns to a full-fledged ideational war against Ethiopia in the global battle for hearts and minds. Egypt and PFJD-Eritrea are now engaged in diplomatic overdrive hell-bent on delegitimizing Ethiopia’s credibility and producing misinformation that materially disadvantage Ethiopia. The regime in Asmara depicts Ethiopia’s measured self-defense as an attempt to control PFDJ-Eritrea’s ports, turn Asmara into an Ethiopian coastal state, and make Addis Ababa a rule maker in the management of the Red Sea. Ethiopia’s peaceful search for sea access is sold by PFDJ-Eritrea and Egypt to the global audience as expansionism, controlling ports and revising the borders of the Horn. This is a scheme to cover up Eritrean incursion and El-Alamein grouping’s support to insurgent groups in Ethiopia. Besides delegitimizing Ethiopia’s reputation, this diplomatic smear campaign organized and directed by El-Alamein bloc is intended to contain Ethiopia as a “landlocked, truncated, weak and circumscribed country.” The El Alamein bloc entails that Egypt seeks to build its Red Sea position on keeping littoral states and non-littoral states apart in order to remake the geography and governance of the Red Sea without Ethiopia. For this to happen, Egypt does so by employing a combination of foreign-policy perceptions, economic pull, security coordination, and military support in the region. The framing of Red Sea for Red Sea littoral states advances closed regionalism and governance unilateralism, embracing Egypt’s conception of Arab Lake. The littoral-centric framing, originated with the formation of the Red Sea Council in 2020, evidently demonstrates the El-Alamein grouping’s policy to exclusively dictate the terms and rules of engagement on all issues of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. This exclusively competitive approach risks producing overlapping security initiatives, diplomatic polarization and uncertainty for trade and investment in the broader region. The ultimate strategic goal of the El-Alamein grouping is all about undermining the peaceful restoration of Ethiopia’s legitimate access to its natural seashores by PFDJ/TPLF assisted by Egypt together with international complicity. That amounts to omitting Ethiopia’s historicity and ontology on the Red Sea. Professor Tecola Hagos captures this grim reality facing the Horn: “With Ethiopia landlocked, the long-term strategy for the Horn is terribly flawed.” With Ethiopia delinked from the Red Sea and barred from the governance of the water strip, the broader Red Sea and Gulf of Aden connected to the Middle East conflict has become a site of contest where land-based powers set to challenge the sea powers and an arena of zero-sum competition. The international community again sticks to the vocabulary and grammar of de-escalation regarding the tensions surrounding Ethiopia and PFDJ-Eritrea. PFDJ-Eritrea’s aversion to talking over fighting which seeks to profit from a contained, landlocked Ethiopia continues to bring insecurity and underdevelopment. Sadly, that war-footing behavior of PFDJ-Eritrea has brought, according to Hassan Umer Abdalla, “a sort of unconsumed divorce and impossible neighborliness” between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Partners with influence should not lose sight of the Eritrean problem fueled by Egypt’s hegemonic ambitions and turbocharged by rival regional security groupings, including, El-Alamein Quadrilateral Security bloc, that intend to corner and stop Ethiopia from ascending. The El-Alamein security arrangement cannot contribute to stability in the region as it is non-transparent, exclusive and negatively directed towards containing Ethiopia’s development. It has already become a source of mistrust Ethiopia perceives it as an instrument for constraining its legitimate national interests. The international partners plunging themselves in the content while leaving the terms of the conversation that trouble the Nile, Horn and Red Sea overlook the regional security logic—logic of dismemberment. The main objective of regional security architecture underpinned by this logic minted by Egypt is all about safeguarding the singular water, maritime and strategic interests against an existential threat from Ethiopia. Although Ethiopia as a resilient civilizational state has turned this logic of dismemberment into a myth, the same logic poses dangers to the security of the Nile and Horn while fueling the already contested wider Red Sea. The moment demands that the Horn of Africa finally break with the regressive regional architecture of “rules by few” and exclusion that continues to constrain and suffocate the future of the region with zero-sum rivalry and bloc politics. It demands that the Horn of Africa embrace tougher, harder, but more enabling paradigm of “rules through dialogue” and institutional inclusion replacing “rules by few” and unilateral governance. This enabling paradigm ensures that regional cooperation does not become a framework for strategic exclusion, opening new possibilities for the countries of the Horn to consult on and shape an open, inclusive regional architecture of mutual enablement that frames security as a shared responsibility and development as a shared empowerment. For this to happen, a new way of imagining agency, doing politics and exercising power is required by the region to deploy native intelligence and negotiate as a collective with the extended neighborhood—broader Arabian Peninsula—and the wider international community to seize the moment. As the global rules are being re-written in the fraying international order for survival and influence, will the Horn of Africa imagine, think and act otherwise to be an author of its future? Ethiopia was one of the world's prominent civilizations in international trade and diplomacy due to its secured sovereign sea access and ports. However, the country had lost its natural, historical, and legal resources due to internal and external political conspiracies as well as various historical circumstances. Efforts being made by the government to address the issue through peaceful and diplomatic means are also showing promising results. The international community has also given due support and attention to Ethiopia's fair demand. In an exclusive interview with ENA, Logistics Researcher Temesgen Walelign said access to the sea plays a significant role in strengthening commercial activities, cargo transport, and global market integration countries. As a result, Ethiopia's lack of port has been incurring additional logistics costs and burdens, preventing products from reaching the global market on time and at competitive prices, he explained. These extra costs affect not only export trade but also cause price hikes on imported goods, ultimately impacting consumers, the researcher added. Moreover, Ethiopia's claim for sea access is appropriate taking into consideration the historical, legal, and long-term development ambitions of the country beyond it geographical location and population. He also praised Ethiopia's efforts in working with neighboring countries to achieve this demand by adhering to principles of give-and-take, peaceful diplomacy, and mutual benefit. Beyond strengthening Ethiopia's commercial and economic capacity, this contributes significantly to fostering lasting regional peace and economic cooperation, Temesgen underscored. Overall, he emphasized that the demand goes beyond current economic needs and forms the foundation of the country's future strategic survival. For his part, the economist Nemomsa Mengesha said Ethiopia's quest for sovereign seaport plays a crucial role in boosting economic competitiveness. ethiopia.title: Prisoner of History, Not Geography
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Prisoner of History, Not Geography - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Prisoner of History, Not Geography 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion Addis Abeba — In early October 2026, Ethiopia and Eritrea took their quarrel to the UN Security Council by letter. Addis Abeba told council members that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 km into Tigray, which Eritrea denies. Asmara replied by calling the accusation a declaration of war and asking the council to take deterrent measures. Ethiopia also alleges that Eritrea is helping fund, mobilize, and direct armed groups in the north. Eritrea, for its part, says Addis Abeba is using its demand for sea access, along with the refrain that Ethiopia "cannot remain a prisoner of geography," as a pretext for military escalation. Officially, Ethiopia says it would pursue access through peace and dialogue. Beneath the exchange of letters lies a misunderstanding of geopolitical theory. When leaders frame Ethiopia, a country of more than 120 million people, as trapped in a landlocked cell by an accident of nature, they borrow shorthand from Tim Marshall's best-selling Prisoners of Geography . It is the kind of snappy line that makes a regional crisis sound like spatial fate. It is a compelling narrative, but it misreads physical geography. Ethiopia's landlocked condition is historical, legal, and political . That is not semantic pedantry; it dictates the cure. If a state is trapped by nature, only brute force or miraculous engineering can break its walls. If it is trapped by human choices, then diplomacy, international law, and regional trade corridors are the proper keys. What a "Prisoner of Geography" actually means Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Marshall's framework applies to immutable physical constraints: terrain that cannot be flattened, climates that cannot be negotiated with, and distances that cannot be erased. Russia is the classic case. Russia's western frontier rests on the North European Plain, a vast flat corridor from Germany to Moscow with no mountain range to stop an invader. Napoleon crossed it in 1812; Hitler in 1941. That vulnerability has driven centuries of Russian effort to push buffer zones westward. On the water, Russia has thousands of miles of coastline but few useful outlets. Murmansk stays ice-free but is hemmed in by the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap. The Black Sea fleet must pass through the Turkish-controlled Bosporus. The Baltic exits squeeze through the Danish straits, and Vladivostok is ice-affected in winter and tucked behind the Japanese archipelago. Catherine the Great's drive to the Black Sea answered this problem, and the problem has outlived her. Whether ruled by a Tsar, a Soviet commissar, or a modern president, the Kremlin keeps getting handed the same geography exam, and the water questions never get easier. This gives us a diagnostic test: a true prisoner of geography remains imprisoned no matter how many times the regime changes, the ideology shifts, or treaties are signed. Consider the rivers of Sub-Saharan Africa. The Congo and the Zambezi carry immense volumes of water, yet rapids, cataracts, and steep escarpments break them into disconnected stretches, preventing continuous navigation from the interior to the sea. Europe's navigable rivers carried goods straight to its ports. No act of parliament or diplomatic summit can persuade a waterfall to flow upstream. Applying the test to Ethiopia Ethiopia fails the test. Its topography is formidable: a volcanic highland massif carved by gorges and split by the Great Rift Valley, which made internal transport a historical challenge. But access to the Red Sea is a different spatial question. The coast is not separated from the highlands by impassable barriers, and Ethiopia has used it. Ethiopia's access to the sea has always been a matter of arrangements, not terrain. It reached the water first by the Franco-Ethiopian railway to Djibouti, which arrived in Addis Abeba in 1917, then, after the 1952 federation with Eritrea, through Assab and Massawa. Even after independence in 1993, cargo kept moving through Assab until the 1998-2000 war closed it. The land never changed. The paperwork did. Ethiopia's access to the sea has always been a matter of arrangements, not terrain." Ethiopia did not lose its coast because tectonic plates threw a tantrum or a mountain range erupted overnight. It lost the sea because of politics , the one force that can relocate a border faster than continental drift. The chain of events is long: Ottoman and Egyptian expansion along the coast; Italian colonization and the creation of Eritrea as a distinct unit; the 1952 UN federation ; the 1962 annexation under Emperor Haile Selassie; a thirty-year war of independence; the 1993 referendum ; and the breakdown of relations in 1998. Every link was a human decision. When Eritrea became independent, Assab became a foreign port, not because the earth shifted but because of a referendum that Ethiopia's own transitional government agreed to and the international community recognized. Ethiopia is not a prisoner of geography. It is a prisoner of history. Global Lessons: Bolivia, Switzerland, and international law The distinction between historical contingency and geographic destiny is well illustrated elsewhere. Bolivia lost its Pacific coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific in the 1880s. Like Ethiopia, it became landlocked through a lost war and later treaties, not because a mountain range rose between its cities and the sea. Bolivia still marks a Day of the Sea each year and keeps a navy on Lake Titicaca, a remarkable act of national memory. Yet when it took Chile to the International Court of Justice , the court ruled in 2018 that Chile had no obligation to negotiate sovereign access. Bolivia's practical economic life has gone on through transit corridors and port facilities on the Chilean and Peruvian coasts. Switzerland, an Alpine nation with no coast, moves its exports down the Rhine to Rotterdam under negotiated transit arrangements with its neighbors. The pattern is clear: where landlocked status is the product of history and borders, commercial access is solved through law, diplomacy, and shared infrastructure, not by claiming a neighbor's territory. International law reflects this. Article 125 of the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees landlocked states a right of access to and from the sea and freedom of transit. It grants a right of transit, not a right to a sovereign coastline. The danger of misdiagnosis Misdiagnosing a political problem as geographic destiny is a dangerous policy mistake. If a nation convinces itself that it sits in a permanent cage imposed by nature, peaceful tools start to look inadequate, and force starts to look like liberation. To be fair to Addis Abeba, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed describes the quest for sea access as irreversible while stressing his commitment to diplomacy. But rhetoric about spatial entitlement has a way of outrunning the diplomacy it promises. The 1998-2000 war killed tens of thousands, devastated both economies, and ended with Ethiopia cut off from Assab, the opposite of its intended effect. Critics will say that Eritrea's own secession shows borders do change. They do, and the difference is consent. Eritrea's independence came through a referendum that Ethiopia's government accepted. Taking a port by force would set a different precedent: that population size or historical grievance justifies redrawing sovereign boundaries. On a continent whose borders were largely drawn by colonial cartographers, that principle would threaten the foundations of the African Union and, in time, Ethiopia's own boundaries. The alternatives are practical, if imperfect. Djibouti handles most of Ethiopia's trade, and diversifying through Berbera, Lamu, and Port Sudan would reduce dependence on it. Each comes with caveats: Berbera lies in Somaliland, whose status Somalia contests, and Port Sudan sits in a country at war. The strongest option is a negotiated commercial arrangement with Eritrea itself, such as port-use rights, shared infrastructure, and trade guarantees, built on the Algiers Agreement framework that both sides signed in 2000. Over-reliance on one corridor through Djibouti burdens Ethiopian businesses, creates strategic vulnerability and constrains a giant economy. Acknowledging that does not require mislabeling its cause. Russia cannot negotiate away the flat open corridor of the North European Plain, and African inland states cannot treaty away river cataracts. Ethiopia can negotiate, build, and trade its way to secure, diversified sea access. Geology may even help eventually: the Afar rift is slowly pulling Africa apart, and some geologists expect a new sea to form there in millions of years. Diplomacy is faster. Ethiopia is not locked in a natural prison. The cell was built by human history, and its door can be opened by human diplomacy. Conclusion The "prisoner of geography" narrative inherently invites military solutions, tempting leaders to enforce their will through force rather than diplomacy. Yet, territory and seaports seized at the barrel of a gun cannot deliver long-term security. True statesmanship lies in converting battlefield leverage into lasting political settlements before war becomes inevitable. Negotiation must not be a desperate last resort pursued only when ammunition is spent, and the economy has collapsed--as the Derg regime learned far too late after squandering its golden opportunities for peace. Real military maturity is measured by using power to forge peace while strong. As Scripture reminds us to remember our Creator in our youth, the optimal time to secure the Horn of Africa's future is during moments of strength. Residents who spoke to Addis Standard accuse the Somali Region Police of shooting at the child and killing her instantly. Meanwhile, residents from the Somali side told Addis Standard that the girl was killed in crossfire between the two sides. Following the incident, elders and security officials reportedly agreed on Monday to remove the Somali Region's flag. However, the decision prompted demonstrations by Somali resident particularly in Kebele 02 on Tuesday that disrupted transport services and forced businesses and bus stations to close amid security fears. Mallicha Diida, a resident of Moyale's Kebele 02, told Addis Standard that the latest incident was part of a recurring cycle of violence in the town. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "In Moyale, human blood has been spilled year after year. Last Sunday, when Somali Regional administration bodies opened a new mayor's office around Kebele 02 and hoisted the Somali Region flag, this act deeply angered many people," he said. Mallicha said gunfire subsequently broke out between Oromia militia members and Somali Region police, prompting the immediate intervention of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), which stopped the exchange. He alleged that Somali Region police shot and killed the 13-year-old girl, describing the incident as an act of "cruelty and lawlessness". He said the officers had killed the child rather than hold those responsible for any alleged wrongdoing accountable, claiming they accused her of throwing stones at them. A resident on the Somali side offered a different account, telling Addis Standard that the Somali-side Moyale town administration had merely relocated its office from its previous premises to a new location. "When they attempted to bring office equipment and hoist the flag, Oromia Region militias opened fire on the Somali Region police to prevent them from succeeding. The young girl was killed in the middle of this, but Somali Region security forces did not target or kill that child," the resident said, rejecting allegations that Somali Region forces were responsible for her death. The agreement was signed on Tuesday in Wuhu, the city in China's Anhui province where Chery is based, between Chery Overseas Investment Corp. and Dahabshiil Motors, the group's vehicle unit. It makes Dahabshiil Motors an authorized Chery dealer in Somalia and includes warranty coverage for buyers, the Somali Embassy in China said in a statement announcing the deal. Hodan Osman Abdi, Somalia's ambassador to China, attended the signing and congratulated both companies. The embassy said the partnership would give Somali consumers access to Chery vehicles backed by warranty services and would strengthen commercial ties between Somali businesses and Chinese manufacturers. The terms of the deal and the Chery models that will be offered were not disclosed. A growing car business Dahabshiil Motors was set up in 2019, when it brought Hyundai to Somaliland as the South Korean carmaker's sole distributor in the Somali regions. It opened with eight Hyundai models, including the Santa Fe, Tucson, Creta and Elantra, along with a commercial bus and a light truck, and built repair and service workshops to support them. Buyers could pay in cash or take Islamic murabaha financing from the group's bank. The unit, which operates in Somaliland and Somalia, has since added Toyota, BYD, JMC and Sinotruk to its range and now sells new vehicles, spare parts, servicing and financing. Chery is its fourth Chinese brand, after BYD, JMC and Sinotruk. Chery, founded in 1997, sold 2.81 million vehicles in 2025 and exported 1.34 million of them, up 17.4% from a year earlier. The company says it has been China's top exporter of passenger vehicles for 23 years in a row. Call for a local plant Abdi used the signing to press Chery to consider building a vehicle plant in Somalia. She pointed to the country's location on the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, its ports and its membership of the East African Community, the regional trade bloc Somalia joined in 2024. She said such an investment could create jobs and build technical skills among young Somalis. The embassy said it would keep working to expand trade and investment between Somalia and China and to help Somali companies gain access to the Chinese market. From remittances to fuel and phones Dahabshiil began in 1970 as a small trading business in Burao, in what is now Somaliland, founded by Duale's father, Mohamed Said Duale. It grew into the largest money transfer company serving the Somali diaspora and now operates in more than 120 countries, with headquarters in Dubai and more than 2,000 employees. Abdirashid Duale, who opened the company's first London branch in 1989, took over as chief executive from his father and has spread the group into banking, telecommunications, energy and real estate. Its holdings include Dahabshil Bank International, which opened in Djibouti in 2009, and a majority stake in Somali telecom operator Somtel, acquired in 2008. In 2023, the group opened the first phase of the Dahabshiil Oil Storage Terminal in the Somaliland port city of Berbera, a facility in which Dahabshiil and its partners have invested more than $100 million. somalia.content: Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Families fleeing Somalia crises find bleak prospects in Dadaab refugee camps Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday October 20, 2026 Nurto fled conflict in Baidoa and is struggling to support her seven children in Dadaab refugee camps/Ahmed Abdulahi/Ergo Families fleeing adversity in different parts of southern Somalia have been arriving in Kenya’s Dadaab refugee camps, where they find themselves with no means of making a living nor aid or support. They include families fleeing conflict in Baidoa, house demolitions by the Somali government in Mogadishu, and drought in their home areas. advertisements The new arrivals say they have received no reception support, shelter, or other forms of aid. Some are staying with relatives already struggling to make ends meet, while others have settled on their own on vacant land in Dadaab’s Ifo-2 camp. They lack food, housing, toilets and other basic services. Nurto Mohamed Ali, who arrived in Ifo-2 on 20 August, said her family had received no assistance and was struggling to meet basic needs. She is staying with relatives who arrived earlier. “Neighbours collect maize and cooking oil for us. That is how we are surviving now,” she said. “We have children who need food and bedding, but we have nothing to give them.” Nurto fled ongoing conflict in Baidoa between federal government forces and those loyal to the former South West State administration. She was a farmer raising her family on their two-hectare plot of land in Baidoa. Separated from her husband, she receives no support from him and is the sole income earner. In the refugee camp now, her seven children often go to bed hungry because she lacks food. They occupy a shelter made from plastic sheets, cloth and thorny branches in the yard of a relatives’ home – a household of 10. The days reach a scorching 37°C and the rainy season has begun. Nurto and her older children have to sleep outside without bedding while the youngest children cram themselves into the hut. Nurto said they had expected to receive assistance on arrival, including refugee registration cards, household items, and a house. She has received nothing. “We have no proper house, and even the people who arrived before us do not have one. The shelter situation is very difficult. We sleep on pieces of cloth and a small, broken mat,” she said. Other vulnerable new arrivals, including older people, people with disabilities, women and children, are finding no formal help in the camp, where some walk around daily asking more established residents for food. Hawo Mohamed Ali, her disabled husband, and their 10 children arrived in Ifo-2 on 1 August. They fled Mogadishu’s Hodan district after the government demolished their house, saying the land belonged to the state. They had lived in the house for 34 years without having formal land ownership documents. She said losing the home made it impossible for her family to remain in Mogadishu. “When we left and went outside, we found our land fenced off and surrounded by a wall,” she told Radio Ergo. “We were told the land would be measured and returned to us. Our houses were demolished using bulldozers, and we thought the land would be given back. Later, we were told it was government land and that we had to leave.” The demolition left Hawo’s family homeless and they decided their only option was to seek refuge in Dadaab. In Mogadishu, she earned a living selling meat and watermelon in local markets. In the refugee camp, however, they have not been registered and haven’t received aid cards or assistance. She looked for laundry work, but the jobs are irregular, so she has to ask others for help with food for her children. She lacks firewood and containers for collecting water. “The children’s father is disabled, and life is very difficult for us. My children are still young and have nothing here. We left our home and came to a place we do not know,” said Hawo, adding that the conditions in Dadaab were far worse than she had expected. The chairman of Hagardera camp, Khalif Dhubow Jelle, said the hardship facing new arrivals from Somalia had been brought to the attention of humanitarian agencies in the camps, but no effective response had followed. He recorded nearly 250 families having arrived from southern Somalia in the past three months. “Their living conditions are extremely poor. It is also the rainy season, yet these people have no shelter or place to stay. They are sitting in the open and have no food or water,” he said. The new arrivals are joining a refugee population already struggling with difficult living conditions because of reduced humanitarian aid and wider economic hardship across the camps. somalia.summary: Families fleeing crises in Somalia are facing dire conditions in the Dadaab refugee camps in Kenya. The camps, originally established to accommodate a temporary influx of refugees, are now home to over 200,000 people, leading to overcrowding and limited resources. Many refugees are struggling with inadequate access to food, clean water, and healthcare. The ongoing conflict, drought, and famine in Somalia have driven families to seek safety, but the camps offer little hope for a better future. Aid organizations are overwhelmed and unable to meet the growing needs of the population, leaving many refugees in a state of uncertainty and despair. The situation highlights the urgent need for international support and sustainable solutions to address the challenges faced by displaced families.

Wiilkeeda Cabdulqaadir Saalax, oo xilligaas toddoba jir ahaa, ayaa firir bir ah kaga haray jirkiisa, waxaana qoysku la kulmay dhibaatooyin la xiriira helitaanka adeeg caafimaad oo ku filan. somalia.title: Kenya’s Ebola Cluster Holds at Nine Cases, but Somalia’s Border Defenses Remain Thin - FTL Somalia
somalia.summary: Kenya's Ministry of Health has confirmed a total of nine Ebola cases linked to a single cluster, with the latest case being a family member of the index patient. All patients are stable and responding well to treatment, with extensive contact tracing successfully identifying 99.3% of contacts. While Kenya has effectively contained the outbreak, Somalia's border defenses remain inadequate, with a WHO assessment indicating only 20% capacity at airports for disease detection. Somalia has initiated a national Ebola preparedness committee and implemented monitoring at airports, but critical gaps in infrastructure and protocols persist. The ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which has surpassed 9,500 cases, poses a significant risk to both countries. Experts warn that without strengthening its health systems, Somalia remains vulnerable to a potential Ebola outbreak.

JSP-Dominated Assembly Convenes in Jowhar to Elect Speaker and President - FTL Somalia
somalia.summary: The newly elected members of Hirshabelle’s House of the People were sworn in on October 21, 2026, in Jowhar, following the Justice and Solidarity Party's (JSP) significant victory in the September 30 elections, where they secured 78 out of 99 seats. This marks the first direct election of regional lawmakers in Hirshabelle, replacing the previous indirect selection system. The assembly is set to elect a speaker and president, with applications for these positions submitted on October 21. However, political tensions persist, particularly regarding the presidency, as the JSP has nominated incumbent President Ali Abdullahi Hussein Guudlaawe, which has sparked disputes with the Hawadle community over representation. While the new parliament represents a procedural advancement, concerns about political inclusivity and legitimacy remain unresolved as the elections proceed.

somalia.title: Four Candidates Contest Galmudug Leadership as JSP’s Dominance Looms Over Election - FTL Somalia
somalia.summary: Four candidates are vying for leadership positions in Galmudug, with the presidential election set for October 22, 2026. The candidates include Liban Ahmed Hassan from the Justice and Solidarity Party (JSP) and Abduqadir Abdullahi Diriye Adawe from the SINCAD Party. During their campaign speeches to the regional parliament, both candidates outlined their priorities, with Hassan focusing on transparency, security, and economic development, while Adawe emphasized education, healthcare, and infrastructure. The election follows a controversial rerun of the parliamentary vote that excluded the Towfiiq political organization, raising questions about the legitimacy of the electoral process. With the JSP holding a significant majority in the assembly, Hassan's victory is widely anticipated, although concerns remain about his ability to govern inclusively given the contentious political backdrop.

It’s Been Lethal. Beyond targeting Rep. Ilhan Omar, the Trump administration has killed, arrested, deported, and demonized Somalis at home and abroad. Nick Turse October 21 2026, 6:00 a.m. ET Share Copy link Share on Facebook Share on Bluesky Share on X Share on LinkedIn Share on WhatsApp Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., in her office on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 10, 2025. Photo: Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post via Getty Images The Trump administration is waging a multi-pronged war on Somali people, painting them as criminals, murderers, and terrorists and using multiple federal agencies to target them at home and abroad. The campaign includes military attacks in Somalia, as well as arrests, deportations, and the weaponization of federal law enforcement agencies against immigrants and the Somali American community in the United States, including the recent use of Homeland Security agents as a goon squad to target Minnesota congresswoman Ilhan Omar. In his second term, President Donald Trump has routinely cast Somalia as lawless and Somalis as violent . Meanwhile, his administration has, largely without public knowledge, killed hundreds of people in Somalia, claiming they belong to terror groups. Trump personally ordered the death of a Somali man within days of regaining the White House, according to his counterterrorism czar Sebastian Gorka. The administration claimed, without offering any evidence, that the man was connected with the Islamic State terror group. Trump has sought to do the same with Omar. Homeland Security agents raided Omar’s Washington, D.C., home last Monday, three weeks before the midterms , in which she is seeking reelection. The Trump administration reportedly launched the investigation to build a case to strip Omar of her U.S. citizenship and ultimately deport her. (Omar fled war in Somalia with her family when she was 8 years old, later immigrated to the U.S. as a refugee , and became a citizen in 2000.) The administration has also issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to some of Omar’s relatives. On Monday, conservative media outlets reported that federal prosecutors obtained Omar’s DNA as part of their investigation. “This is what happens in a dictatorship. The leader identifies his political, ethnic and religious enemies, and his agents scramble to do his bidding and make him happy,” Zaynab Mohamed, a Somali immigrant who represents Minneapolis in Minnesota’s state Senate, told The Intercept. “Representative Omar is the latest subject where Trump identifies the target and his minions go looking for a crime. The cases always fall apart, and this one will, too.” Related DHS Was Designed as a Weapon Trump claimed not to have ordered the raid, but throughout his second term, his Justice Department has repeatedly targeted his political enemies — from New York’s attorney general , to the former head of the FBI, to members of the Federal Reserve. “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ,” Trump said to reporters. “I have nothing to do with it.” Omar called it “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” She added: “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” Omar’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment from The Intercept. With the Somali community , Trump found a target that he could attack with Islamophobic, racist, and xenophobic rhetoric , without incurring much mainstream backlash, said Jaylani Hussein, the executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations. “As immigrants, Muslims, and — most importantly — Black people, it’s the trifecta,” he told The Intercept. “None of us expected the scale and level of the vitriol. But despite this, it’s at the point that the traditional media almost ignore the attacks on the Somali-American community because it’s not a large constituency. Trump says these things, and people just move on.” Most Read Inside ICE, Officials Question String of Trump Admin “Midterm Panic Moves” Karl Loftus Lockheed Martin Showered Susan Collins With Cash as F-35 Program Hit Turbulence Noah Hurowitz President Apocalypse Tom Engelhardt Trump’s War on Somalia Over the last decade, Trump has overseen the killing of as many as 1,500 Somalis in more than 400 attacks, according to a count by New America, a D.C.-based think tank. During his second term alone, the Trump administration has conducted more than 200 airstrikes in Somalia, including close to 90 this year, claiming to target terrorists. The U.S. military has been at war in Somalia for almost a quarter-century, conducting air attacks and commando raids aimed at the terrorist group al-Shabab as well as the Islamic State group, while the CIA and special operators created local proxy forces to conduct low-profile operations on behalf of America. At the same time, the U.S. has provided Somalia with billions of dollars in counterterrorism assistance. Related U.S. Conducts “Largest Airstrike in the History of the World” (Sort Of) U.S. attacks in Somalia have skyrocketed during Trump’s terms in office. From 2007 to 2017, under the administrations of George W. Bush and Barack Obama, the U.S. military carried out 59 declared airstrikes in Somalia. The Biden administration conducted 51 declared strikes over four years. During Trump’s six years in office, the U.S. has launched more than 400 attacks against purported militants. The U.S. rarely offers any evidence that those killed are members of terrorist groups, much less leaders. A New America analysis found militant leaders comprised just 1.7 percent of those killed. Africa Command refused to provide requested evidence that any of those killed in airstrikes in Somalia this year were militants. “All U.S. strikes in Somalia are conducted in close coordination partners [sic] against designated terror groups,” an AFRICOM spokesperson told The Intercept by email. “Trump has conducted more drone strikes in Somalia than Bush, Obama, and Biden combined. And so many civilians have died,” historian Elizabeth Schmidt, the author of “Foreign Intervention in Africa After the Cold War: Sovereignty, Responsibility, and the War on Terror,” told The Intercept. “They were often just young men living in an area where it was easy to label them jihadis. And it turns out they had nothing to do with terrorism.” The U.S. claims that it has only killed six civilians over almost two decades of war in Somalia. A count by the airstrike monitoring group Airwars put the number at as much as 2,600 percent higher . A 2023 investigation by The Intercept determined, for example, that a drone attack in Somalia during Trump’s first term killed at least three, and possibly five, civilians, including 22-year-old Luul Dahir Mohamed and her 4-year-old daughter Mariam Shilow Muse. At the time of the attack, the U.S. announced it had killed “ five terrorists ” and that “no civilians were killed in this airstrike.” Trump calls Somalia a “third-world” or “ fourth-world nation ,” says that it “ stinks ,” and disparaged Somalis who come to the U.S., saying “we’re going to go the wrong way if we keep taking in garbage into our country.” His most xenophobic consigliere also claims Somalia is responsible for violence that has caused people to flee the country. “The entire Somali refugee program is predicated on a lie,” wrote Trump’s deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, Stephen Miller, late last year. “Destroying your own country does not give you the right to become a citizen in ours.” But this faux history disregards America’s decadeslong role in fomenting violence in Somalia and destabilizing the country. “The presence of Somalis in the U.S. has a lot to do with U.S. wars in Somalia.” A casualty of the Cold War geopolitics that led to widespread conflict, political repression, and millions of deaths across the developing world, Somalia has experienced persistent political instability and strife since the late 1960s. In recent decades, the country has suffered civil war, famine, droughts, a longtime al-Shabab insurgency, and persistent humanitarian crises. Related Who Could Have Predicted the U.S. War in Somalia Would Fail? The Pentagon. Over the last quarter century, the U.S. has intensified conflict in Somalia through direct attacks; training, funding, and running proxy forces; and funneling in weapons and other military assistance to one side of a civil war. As early as 2007, the Pentagon was aware that there were fundamental flaws with U.S. military operations in the Horn of Africa, and Somalia devolved into another forever war stalemate. This has continued, despite the record number of airstrikes in Somalia under Trump. Before Trump took office, in 2016, Islamist militants in Somalia killed 4,281 people , according to the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, a Pentagon research institution. By August, this year’s total hit 6,731 deaths, a 57 percent increase. An analysis by the Costs of War project at Brown University found that instead of eliminating militant groups, the U.S. counterterrorism campaign in Somalia was “ensuring that the conflict continues in perpetuity.” An AFRICOM spokesperson said the command’s “operational focus remains on working with partners to degrade terrorist organizations to create the space required for Somali-led governance and stability.” But Trump claims Somalia has no government , no military , and is “ not even a country .” “ They weren’t coming because they wanted a better job. It’s because they feared for their lives and their children’s lives.” The Intercept interviewed people displaced by the forever war in a camp on the outskirts of Somalia’s capital, Mogadishu, in 2023. “We had to leave because of the drought and the conflict,” a mother of seven told this reporter. She was one of more than a dozen women from the Lower Shabelle region of southwest Somalia who spoke to The Intercept after fleeing the front lines of an offensive by the U.S.-backed Somali government against al-Shabab. Since Trump first took office, the number of Somalis forced from their homes has almost doubled from 2.4 million to 4.4 million. “I don’t think most Americans realize that the presence of Somalis in the U.S. has a lot to do with U.S. wars in Somalia. U.S. military intervention made a bad situation worse. This led to a surge of refugees and asylum-seekers to the U.S.,” said Schmidt. “They weren’t coming because they wanted a better job. It’s because they feared for their lives and their children’s lives.” During Trump’s first term, his administration acknowledged “ the ongoing armed conflict ” as a reason to extend temporary protected status — which grants legal status, work authorization, and protection from deportation — to Somalis in the U.S., noting the security situation was “fragile and volatile, with ongoing armed conflict among government forces, clan militias, African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) troops, and al-Shabaab.” We’re independent of corporate interests — and powered by members.
